newsitem.title: UKRAINE: FOCUS-Ukraine parliament passes delayed 1997 budget.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Ukraine parliament passes delayed 1997 budget.

text.p: Ukraine's parliament passed the much-delayed 1997 budget by 229 votes to 71 on Friday, approving a deficit of 5.7 percent of gross domestic product or 4.0 percent by International Monetary Fund (IMF) standards.
Deputies set revenues at 22.4 billion hryvnias ($12 billion) and expenditures at 28.12 billion hryvnias in line with IMF demands. There were 11 abstentions and 27 no votes.
The Fund is waiting for Ukraine to meet 41 conditions to give it a $2.5-$3 billion, three-year Extended Fund Facility (EFF) to succeed an $867 million stand-by loan which expired in February.
But the IMF told Reuters on Friday that the Fund was considering a temporary stand-by agreement to tide Ukraine over until it met all the conditions.

"The budget is a good step but it's not sufficient for the EFF," Senior Resident Representative Patrick Lenain said, adding that Ukraine would still have to cut payroll taxes from 52 percent to 40 percent as a first step.
An estimated 60 percent of the economy goes undeclared and the IMF wants Ukraine to legalise it by cutting punitive taxes.
The Ukrainian side said recently it had met 27 of the conditions, but the budget was key.
On the expenditures side about 2.2 billion hryvnias was set aside for social benefits payments, and government support to the coal sector was 1.0 billion hryvnias.
A further 1.5 billion hryvnias was earmarked to help clear a mountain of wage arrears which has sparked street protests.
Inflation has been forecast in budget papers at 25 percent but recently officials have said it will be about 17 percent.
This year the former Soviet republic expects to post its first growth since independence of 0.3 percent this year after the economy contracted by 10 percent last year.
Ukraine has never passed a budget by January 1 since it won independence from Moscow in 1991 but this was a record delay.
For the first time deputies banned covering the deficit with central bank credits, cancelling an earlier vote on the last day of budget debates.
They also placed no limits on revenues from foreign credits, expected to cover 2.4 billion hryvnias of the deficit, but deputies will have to approve each loan.

Parliament has passed two out of nine tax laws underpinning the budget, on valued added tax and levies on business profits, but all nine have been requested by the IMF and parliament plans to consider them once it reconvenes in September.

It was the tax reforms which held up the budget, keeping it in legislative limbo for months between government and the communist-dominated parliament, which approved the draft at a first reading last December but sent it back for amendments.
The tax laws were proposed by former deputy prime minister Viktor Pynzenyk who resigned in disgust two months ago, blaming both sides for lacking the political will to pass reforms.
Pynzenyk, seeking to eradicate widespread corruption among government officials, had proposed reforms which would have removed the need for licenses for foreign investors.
They would also have closed a loophole which allows technically bankrupt businesses to dodge the law by declaring they cannot pay taxes. ($ = 1.856 Ukrainian Hryvnias)
